clue.text: Taken by the champion angler?

parts.note: the best angler 'takes the cake', and an angler's cake would be made of his catch

explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'takes the cake' means wins or outdoes everyone, so the winning angler takes a cake made from fish.
explanation.definitionFit: A patty of flaked fish and potato is the dish named, a cake of fish.

clue.text: This dance should be a blooming success

definitions.text: This dance should be a blooming success

parts.words: This dance should be a blooming success
parts.note: the Helston Furry, a Cornish processional dance, has a name suggesting flowers

explanation.walkthrough: The Helston dance in Cornwall is known by a name meaning of flowers, so it should bloom.
explanation.definitionFit: The Cornish spring dance has a name meaning of flowers, fitting blooming.

clue.text: They didn't succeed in saving their skins

definitions.text: They didn't succeed in saving their skins

parts.words: They didn't succeed in saving their skins
parts.note: the bones left after death have lost their skin, read literally

explanation.walkthrough: 'saving their skins' means escaping, but read literally the bony frames kept none of their skin.
explanation.definitionFit: Bony frames left after the flesh is gone have no skin at all.

clue.text: Not a straightforward feature of town planning

definitions.text: Not a straightforward feature of town planning

parts.words: Not a straightforward feature of town planning
parts.note: a curved terrace of houses in a town is not straight

explanation.walkthrough: 'straightforward' means simple, but here it is literal: not straight, a curved street.
explanation.definitionFit: A curved row of houses or street, shaped like a new moon.

clue.text: Crossword

parts.note: an X, the cross, stands for this word at the foot of a letter

explanation.walkthrough: An X written at the end of a letter stands for a kiss, so a cross is that word.
explanation.definitionFit: The X sign at a letter's end means a kiss.

clue.text: A pill if taken the wrong way can be stimulating

definitions.note: the clue says the thing 'can be stimulating'; the answer is the noun for a boost

indicators.note: read backwards, the words pill if are taken in the wrong direction

explanation.surface: A warning about swallowing a tablet badly, which turns out to give a jolt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taken the wrong way' turns PILLIF round. 'A ... can be stimulating' frames the noun: a stimulus.
explanation.definitionFit: A fillip is a boost or stimulus, something that rouses or invigorates.

clue.text: Batting companion?

parts.note: at cricket a batsman's partner is also 'in'

explanation.walkthrough: In cricket both batsmen at the crease are 'in'; split as IN MATE, while the word means a prisoner.
explanation.definitionFit: A resident of a prison or asylum; here a mate who is in.

clue.text: " Therefore 'tis meet That noble minds keep ever with their —— " (J. Caesar)

definitions.text: Therefore 'tis meet That noble minds keep ever with their

parts.words: Therefore 'tis meet That noble minds keep ever with their
parts.note: Cassius in Julius Caesar says noble minds should keep company with their equals

explanation.walkthrough: Fill in Cassius's line (Act 1, scene 2): noble minds should keep with others like them.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare uses the plural noun for one's equals or kind, people similar to oneself.

clue.text: No need to exhort him to "hang on"

definitions.text: No need to exhort him to "hang on"

parts.words: No need to exhort him to "hang on"
parts.note: a sponger clings to a host by nature, so needs no encouragement to hang on

explanation.walkthrough: 'hang on' means wait, but a sponger or leech literally hangs on to others.
explanation.definitionFit: A sponger lives off a host, clinging to it.

clue.text: Their opponents in the ring are a beefy lot

definitions.text: Their opponents in the ring are a beefy lot

parts.words: Their opponents in the ring are a beefy lot
parts.note: the ring is a bullring, and the beefy opponents are bulls, not boxers

explanation.walkthrough: 'ring' and 'beefy' suggest boxing heavyweights; the opponents are bulls, beef on the hoof.
explanation.definitionFit: Bullfighters face bulls in the arena.

clue.text: What makes a bee so fat?

indicators.note: what the letters of bee so make when rearranged is the word wanted

explanation.surface: A child's riddle asking why a bee is so plump.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What makes' is the anagram signal: BEESO rearranged; the 'a' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Obese means grossly overweight, very stout.

clue.text: The last man to know the answer to " What's afoot? "

definitions.text: The last man to know the answer to " What's afoot? "

parts.words: The last man to know the answer to " What's afoot? "
parts.note: a last is the foot-shaped block a cobbler works on, and the man at it knows all about what is on a foot

explanation.walkthrough: 'The last man' looks like 'the least likely person', but a last is a cobbler's wooden foot form; 'What's afoot?' means what is on the foot.
explanation.definitionFit: A cobbler works at a last making footwear, so he would know what goes on a foot.

clue.text: It's just fine

parts.note: reads as 'all is well', but means the act of imposing a penalty payment, which is just

explanation.walkthrough: 'fine' is a verb here, to levy a money penalty, not 'all right'.
explanation.definitionFit: To amerce is an old legal word for punishing someone by a monetary penalty.

clue.text: They spend some time at drawing, but know just when to stop

definitions.text: They spend some time at drawing, but know just when to stop

parts.words: They spend some time at drawing, but know just when to stop
parts.note: drawing is pulling teeth, and stopping is filling cavities, not sketching

explanation.walkthrough: Drawing (extracting teeth) and stopping (an old word for filling a tooth) are both surgery jobs; the surface suggests artists.
explanation.definitionFit: Tooth doctors extract teeth and fill cavities, the drawing and stopping named.

clue.text: Singular clerical garb?

parts.note: clergy vestments are called by a plural noun, so one item would be the singular

explanation.walkthrough: Canonicals (plural) are a clergyman's robes; the singular of that word is the adjective meaning according to church law.
explanation.definitionFit: Clerical robes are called canonicals; the singular form means conforming to church canon.

clue.text: In the direction of the Netherlands?

definitions.text: In the direction of the Netherlands?

parts.words: In the direction of the Netherlands?
parts.note: nether means lower, so the nether lands are the lands below

explanation.walkthrough: 'Netherlands' is split into 'nether lands', the lower regions, so heading there is heading lower.
explanation.definitionFit: Heading towards lower regions means moving toward the ground, below.

clue.text: Take it off, it's hot!

indicators.note: taking it off means the letters of the word it are removed

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone urging another to remove a garment because the weather is warm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off' removes IT from ITSHOT. A take is one filmed or photographed attempt.
explanation.definitionFit: In film-making a single recorded take is also called a shot.

clue.text: Past-master?

parts.note: a past master is an expert, but here it is a master of the past

explanation.walkthrough: A 'past master' is an expert; read it as a master of the past, a scholar of bygone times.
explanation.definitionFit: A scholar who studies and writes about the past.

clue.text: Kitchener's dance here?

parts.note: a kitchener is one who works in a kitchen, so a cook's; the surface suggests Lord Kitchener
a hop is an informal dance

explanation.surface: Wondering whether Lord Kitchener held a ball at this place.
explanation.walkthrough: Lord Kitchener was a famous British field marshal; here a kitchener is simply a cook.
explanation.definitionFit: An eating house where food is cooked and sold.

clue.text: Ten Scots in Highland games, perhaps

indicators.note: Ten Scots taking part in the games are mixed together into the word wanted

explanation.surface: Ten Scotsmen competing at a gathering in the Highlands.
explanation.walkthrough: TENSCOTS rearranges; the Highland games are a Scottish sports meeting.
explanation.definitionFit: The Highland games are a set of competitions, an example of the plural.

clue.text: "Fast by the banks of the slow winding-" (Cowper)

definitions.text: "Fast by the banks of the slow winding-" (Cowper)

parts.words: "Fast by the banks of the slow winding-" (Cowper)
parts.note: a line from William Cowper's poem The Task, ending on the name of a river by his home at Olney

explanation.walkthrough: Fill in the missing word of Cowper's line from The Task: the Great Ouse flows slowly past Olney in Buckinghamshire, where he lived.
explanation.definitionFit: Cowper's line names the slow English river at Olney, the Great Ouse.

clue.text: Its inhabitants were by no means distinguished

definitions.text: Its inhabitants were by no means distinguished

parts.words: Its inhabitants were by no means distinguished
parts.note: 'by no means' is read as 'by having no money', the mark of residents of a workhouse

explanation.walkthrough: 'by no means' seems to be 'not at all', but it says the residents were distinguished by having no means, no money.
explanation.definitionFit: A workhouse housed paupers, people marked out by their lack of money.

clue.text: Right place for the wake

parts.note: a ship's wake trails behind it, not a funeral gathering

explanation.walkthrough: 'wake' suggests a funeral vigil; it is the track a ship leaves behind it.
explanation.definitionFit: A vessel's wake lies behind it, toward the rear.

clue.text: A penny one is one

parts.note: a ... is a unit of mass for gold and silver

explanation.walkthrough: A pennyweight is an old unit of mass (one twentieth of a troy ounce).
explanation.definitionFit: A pennyweight is a unit of heaviness, so this is a measure of mass.

clue.text: The "Royal George", for example?

parts.note: the Royal George was a famous warship, and a King George is a royal George

explanation.walkthrough: HMS Royal George was a warship that sank in 1782; split the answer as KING'S HIP, a ship of the king, while the word means royal rank.
explanation.definitionFit: Royal status or rule, the office of a monarch, is what a Royal George holds.

clue.text: Could she be the girl for Colonel Sebastian?

indicators.note: could she be suggests the letters may be made into her name

parts.note: Colonel Sebastian Moran is Moriarty's henchman in the Sherlock Holmes stories

explanation.surface: Wondering whether a certain woman is right for an army colonel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Could she be' asks for MORAN rearranged: Colonel Sebastian Moran is the villain in Conan Doyle's The Empty House.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman's given name, here supplied as the girl.

clue.text: Made an effort to confuse the electorate

indicators.note: confusing the letters mixes them into a new order

parts.note: the electorate are the voters

explanation.surface: A politician tried hard to muddle the public.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to confuse' rearranges VOTERS, the word the electorate stands for, not the printed words.
explanation.definitionFit: Strove is the past tense of strive, to try hard.

clue.text: Chief feature of an ecclesiastical court

explanation.surface: The main feature of a church court.
explanation.definitionFit: Arch means chief, as in archbishop; the Court of Arches is the Church of England's court for Canterbury.

clue.text: It's removed in the dock

parts.note: docking a horse cuts its tail short, so the hair goes; the surface suggests a courtroom dock

explanation.walkthrough: 'dock' looks like the courtroom box or a harbour, but to dock is to cut short a horse's tail.
explanation.definitionFit: When a horse's tail is docked, the long tail hair is cut away.

clue.text: Just the kind of music for the playground

explanation.surface: Someone recommending the right tunes for children at play.
explanation.definitionFit: Swing is a jazz style of the 1930s, and also a seat hung on ropes for children to ride.

clue.text: But people living in them might still have their ups and downs

definitions.text: But people living in them might still have their ups and downs

parts.words: But people living in them might still have their ups and downs
parts.note: flat lands have no hills, yet residents still have good and bad times

explanation.walkthrough: 'ups and downs' means life's fortunes, contrasted with the flatness of the land.
explanation.definitionFit: Plains are wide flat areas of land without hills.

clue.text: One of the fruits of repetition

definitions.text: One of the fruits of repetition

parts.words: One of the fruits of repetition
parts.note: a stale, much-repeated joke is called by the name of a tree nut

explanation.walkthrough: A tired old joke told too often is called by the name of a nut, a fruit of repetition.
explanation.definitionFit: A tree nut that is also slang for a stale, overused story.
